approaches.name: Open anterior approach to the clavicle
approaches.corridor: Subclavicular incision through platysma and clavipectoral fascia to the anterior or anteroinferior clavicle

sources.title: Superior versus anteroinferior plating for displaced midshaft clavicle fractures
Anterior inferior plating versus superior plating for clavicle fracture

procedure_applications.condition: A shaft or selected medial fracture requires open reduction with anterior or anteroinferior plate application

positioning.text: Position beach-chair or supine on a radiolucent table with the scapula supported and the shoulder freely mobile for reduction of the lateral fragment.

setup.text: Prep the neck, shoulder, and arm; ensure fluoroscopic visualization of the entire clavicle and use guarded drilling because the plexus and subclavian vessels lie deep to the medial-middle junction.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, palpable clavicle, fracture, and planned plate span.

incision.text: Make an oblique incision approximately 8–10 cm long just inferior to and centered on the fracture, curving as needed for medial fixation.

superficial_interval.text: Divide and tag platysma, identify and preserve supraclavicular nerve branches, then open clavipectoral fascia with minimal flap elevation.

deep_interval.text: Expose the anterior clavicle between pectoralis major anteriorly and trapezius posteriorly, preserving periosteal and muscular attachments on comminuted fragments.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, platysma, supraclavicular sensory branches, clavipectoral fascia and periosteum, then clavicle.

structures_encountered.text: Platysma, supraclavicular nerves, clavipectoral fascia, pectoralis major, trapezius, subclavius and periosteum define the exposure.

structures_at_risk.text: Supraclavicular sensory nerves, subclavian vessels, brachial plexus, pleura, and fragment blood supply are at risk.

danger_zones.text: At the medial-middle junction, keep sharp instruments and drill tips controlled against the far cortex; do not sweep blindly beneath the clavicle.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid fixed deep retractors beneath the clavicle and excessive traction on preserved supraclavicular branches or devascularized comminution.

exposure.text: Provides broad visualization of shaft morphology and permits either anterior or superior plate placement through the same general exposure.

limitations.text: Open exposure increases scar and sensory disturbance and risks fragment devascularization if comminution is stripped; plating surface has no universal outcome advantage.

extensions.text: Extend medially or laterally along the clavicle for fixation while preserving ligament and muscle attachments not required for reduction.

indications.text: Applicable to most clavicular shaft fractures selected for open fixation and to selected medial patterns requiring direct reduction.

relative_contraindications.text: Favor a limited or alternative method when indirect reduction is acceptable, the soft-tissue envelope is compromised, or full open visualization would unnecessarily strip comminution.

implant_implications.text: Contour an anterior or anteroinferior plate to the S-shaped clavicle, obtain balanced fixation on both main fragments, and use guarded drilling and measured bicortical screws.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm length, alignment, rotation, plate position, screw length, and avoidance of sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints.

closure.text: Cover the plate with a secure clavipectoral fascial-periosteal repair, precisely reapproximate platysma, and close skin without tension.

complications.text: Complications include supraclavicular numbness or neuroma, vascular or plexus injury, pneumothorax, infection, nonunion, hardware irritation or failure, and reoperation.

bailouts.text: If safe far-cortex control or reduction cannot be achieved, enlarge exposure under direct vision or change plate position rather than drilling or clamping blindly.

questions.question: Which deep structures are most vulnerable near the medial-middle clavicle?
questions.answer: The subclavian artery and vein, brachial plexus, and pleura.

questions.question: Which sensory nerves should be preserved?
Why preserve soft-tissue attachments to comminution?
questions.answer: To maintain fragment perfusion and support union.

approaches.name: Minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis approach to the clavicle
approaches.corridor: Two short end incisions joined by a blunt epiperiosteal tunnel for anterior or superior bridge plating

sources.title: MIPO anterior approach to the clavicle
Complications and clinical outcomes with MIPO for midshaft clavicle fractures
Minimally invasive plate osteosynthesis for clavicle fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A midshaft fracture is suitable for indirect reduction and bridge plating with preservation of intermediate fragments

positioning.text: Position beach-chair or supine with the scapula supported and the arm mobile to restore clavicular length and alignment indirectly.

setup.text: Template plate length and location before incision, prep the entire clavicle and arm, and ensure continuous fluoroscopic visualization of both ends and the fracture.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark both clavicular ends, fracture zone, planned plate ends and holes, sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, and supraclavicular nerve territory.

incision.text: Make separate medial and lateral incisions approximately 2–3 cm long over the planned plate ends, adding only targeted stab incisions for screws or reduction tools.

superficial_interval.text: Protect visible supraclavicular branches, open fascia locally, and create a blunt subcutaneous or epiperiosteal tunnel connecting the end windows.

deep_interval.text: Pass the plate through the prepared tunnel without stripping the fracture zone, using a small direct fracture window only if indirect reduction fails.

layers.text: Skin and subcutaneous tissue at two windows, supraclavicular nerve branches, local fascia and periosteum, blunt tunnel, then main clavicular fragments.

structures_encountered.text: Supraclavicular nerves, platysma, clavipectoral fascia, periosteum and the medial and lateral main fragments are encountered; intermediate fragments remain covered.

structures_at_risk.text: Supraclavicular nerves, subclavian vessels, brachial plexus, pleura, and skin over the tunneled plate are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Tunnel and drill under controlled contact with bone; never pass instruments blindly deep to the clavicle or across the medial-middle junction.

retraction_hazards.text: Avoid forceful retraction through short incisions, which can injure sensory branches or skin; extend a window when visualization is inadequate.

exposure.text: Exposes the main fragments and plate endpoints while preserving fracture hematoma and soft-tissue attachments around comminution.

limitations.text: Indirect reduction makes length, axis, and rotation harder to judge and is poorly suited when anatomic reduction of a simple fracture or direct debridement is essential.

extensions.text: Add a limited fracture-site incision for a blocking fragment or irreducible deformity, or convert to the full open approach when safe reduction cannot be verified.

indications.text: Best suited to selected multifragmentary midshaft fractures where relative stability and biologic preservation are desired; some simple patterns may qualify when soft-tissue considerations favor MIPO.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid for medial or lateral patterns outside the implant design, gross contamination, neurovascular exploration, or a simple pattern requiring direct anatomic compression when indirect control is unreliable.

implant_implications.text: Use a sufficiently long bridge plate with balanced fixation in both main fragments, confirm plate centering, and protect deep structures during every percutaneous screw pass.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Imaging must confirm clavicular length, coronal and sagittal alignment, rotation, plate location, endpoint fixation, and safe screw lengths.

closure.text: Close each fascial window securely over the plate, incorporating preserved periosteum when possible, then close skin without tension.

complications.text: Complications include malalignment or shortening, supraclavicular numbness, vascular or plexus injury, pneumothorax, infection, nonunion, implant failure or prominence, and skin compromise.

bailouts.text: If fluoroscopy cannot prove length and rotation or the plate cannot pass safely, open the fracture deliberately rather than persisting with blind tunneling.

questions.question: How many principal incisions are used for clavicle MIPO?
questions.answer: Two short incisions over the medial and lateral plate ends.

questions.question: What biology does MIPO preserve?
questions.answer: Fracture hematoma and soft-tissue attachments to intermediate fragments.

approaches.name: Medial-entry intramedullary nailing approach to the clavicle
approaches.corridor: Small anterior medial-clavicle window into the intramedullary canal for lateral nail passage

sources.title: Intramedullary nailing versus plate fixation for displaced midshaft clavicle fractures
Plate fixation or intramedullary fixation for midshaft clavicle fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A selected midshaft fracture can be reduced and stabilized with an intramedullary device

positioning.text: Position beach-chair or supine with the shoulder supported, medial clavicle accessible, and arm mobile for indirect reduction.

setup.text: Prepare the full clavicle and arm, template nail diameter and length, and obtain clear fluoroscopic views of the medial entry, fracture, and lateral fragment.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the sternoclavicular joint, medial clavicle, fracture, lateral clavicle, and anticipated anterior nail entry just lateral to the joint.

incision.text: Make a 1–2 cm anterior incision just lateral to the sternoclavicular joint over the medial clavicular entry point.

superficial_interval.text: Bluntly dissect to bone, protecting supraclavicular sensory branches and maintaining direct contact with the anterior clavicle.

deep_interval.text: Create the medial canal entry under direct and fluoroscopic control, then advance the flexible nail along the S-shaped canal without perforating cortex.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue and supraclavicular branches, fascia and periosteum, medial clavicular cortex, then intramedullary canal.

structures_encountered.text: Supraclavicular sensory branches, platysma, medial clavicle, sternoclavicular-adjacent soft tissues, canal, and fracture are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Supraclavicular nerves, sternoclavicular joint, subclavian vessels, brachial plexus, pleura, and skin at the medial nail end are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Do not direct the entry tool or nail posteriorly beyond the far cortex; avoid medial migration toward the sternoclavicular region and intrathoracic structures.

retraction_hazards.text: Use minimal retraction through the small medial window and enlarge it if the entry point cannot be seen directly.

exposure.text: Provides limited medial canal access with indirect fracture reduction and little fracture-site stripping.

limitations.text: The curved canal and comminution can impede passage, rotational control is less direct than plating, and some patterns require a small fracture-site incision.

extensions.text: Add a limited fracture window for reduction or nail passage, or convert to plate fixation when canal passage or stable alignment cannot be achieved.

indications.text: Use for selected displaced midshaft fractures with a canal and pattern suitable for intramedullary fixation; technique choice remains patient- and fracture-specific.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid in markedly comminuted, very medial or lateral, canal-incompatible, pathologic, or irreducible patterns lacking reliable length and rotational control.

implant_implications.text: Select a nail that negotiates the canal without cortical perforation, seat the medial end to minimize skin irritation, and secure it against migration according to device design.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Continuously confirm entry, intramedullary passage, fracture reduction, lateral endpoint, absence of cortical perforation, and final nail position.

closure.text: Irrigate, verify the nail end is not prominent beneath skin, close fascia and skin in layers, and protect the medial entry wound.

complications.text: Complications include cortical perforation, nail migration, medial skin irritation, supraclavicular neuropathy, pneumothorax or neurovascular injury, malalignment, nonunion, infection, and implant removal.

bailouts.text: Stop if the nail leaves the canal or cannot cross safely; use a targeted fracture window, exchange the implant, or convert to plating rather than forcing passage.

questions.question: Where is the standard clavicle nail entry incision?
questions.answer: Anteriorly just lateral to the sternoclavicular joint.

questions.question: What geometric feature makes nail passage difficult?
What must never be accepted during nail passage?
questions.answer: Posterior cortical perforation or extraosseous advancement toward neurovascular and thoracic structures.

approaches.name: Open superior approach to the clavicle
approaches.corridor: Supraclavicular incision through platysma and clavipectoral fascia to the superior clavicle

sources.title: Superior versus anteroinferior plating for displaced midshaft clavicle fractures
Anteroinferior versus superior plating for midshaft clavicle fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A lateral, shaft, or medial fracture requires direct superior exposure and superior plate fixation

positioning.text: Position beach-chair or supine with scapular support and free shoulder motion to elevate the lateral fragment during reduction.

setup.text: Prep the neck, shoulder, and arm; ensure whole-clavicle imaging and use drill stops or guarded technique to protect the deep plexus, vessels, and pleura.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark sternoclavicular and acromioclavicular joints, clavicular borders, fracture, deltoid attachment laterally, and planned superior plate span.

incision.text: Make an oblique 8–10 cm incision directly superior to and centered on the fracture, extending as needed for medial or lateral patterns.

superficial_interval.text: Raise limited anterior and posterior subcutaneous flaps, identify and preserve supraclavicular sensory branches, and open clavipectoral fascia.

deep_interval.text: Reflect only the pectoralis or deltoid attachment required for plate seating, keeping lateral deltoid as a contiguous repairable sheet and preserving fragment soft tissues.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, platysma and supraclavicular nerves, clavipectoral fascia and periosteum, deltoid or pectoral attachment as required, then superior clavicle.

structures_encountered.text: Platysma, supraclavicular nerves, clavipectoral fascia, pectoralis major, trapezius, deltoid laterally, periosteum, and clavicle are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Supraclavicular sensory branches, subclavian vessels, brachial plexus, pleura, deltoid attachment, and fragment perfusion are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Superior-to-inferior drilling points toward critical infraclavicular structures; maintain direct far-cortex control and avoid deep plunging, especially medially.

retraction_hazards.text: Do not place unprotected retractors under the clavicle or tension preserved sensory nerves; expand exposure rather than increasing deep pressure.

exposure.text: Provides direct access across lateral, shaft, and medial clavicle and a straight view for superior plate contouring and application.

limitations.text: Superior implants can be prominent beneath thin skin, and comparative evidence does not show a universal union or functional advantage over anteroinferior plating.

extensions.text: Extend along the superior clavicle, reflecting deltoid or pectoral tissue only where required and preserving AC and coracoclavicular ligament attachments when intact.

indications.text: Applicable to lateral, diaphyseal, and medial clavicle fractures selected for open reduction, with superior plating especially common for lateral patterns.

relative_contraindications.text: Consider anteroinferior or limited fixation when superior hardware prominence, scar location, compromised superior skin, or the required drill trajectory is unfavorable.

implant_implications.text: Contour the plate to the superior S-curve, obtain balanced fragment fixation, avoid AC or SC joint penetration, and use guarded bicortical drilling.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm length, alignment, rotation, articular-joint clearance, plate contour, and safe screw lengths across the entire construct.

closure.text: Repair reflected deltoid or pectoral attachments, cover the plate with clavipectoral fascia and periosteum, precisely reapproximate platysma, and close skin without tension.

complications.text: Complications include sensory numbness or neuroma, prominent hardware and removal, deep vascular or plexus injury, pneumothorax, deltoid dysfunction, infection, nonunion, and implant failure.

bailouts.text: If superior drilling cannot be protected or soft-tissue coverage is inadequate, reposition the plate anteroinferiorly or change fixation strategy rather than accepting unsafe screws or exposed hardware.

questions.question: Which fractures are commonly plated superiorly?
questions.answer: Lateral clavicle fractures, although shaft and medial fractures may also use superior fixation.

questions.question: What sensory complication follows supraclavicular nerve injury?
questions.answer: Numbness or a painful proximal neuroma.

questions.question: Why avoid stripping comminuted fragments?
questions.answer: Maintaining their soft-tissue blood supply is more important than perfect reduction of every fragment.
